name: SaaSAudit
author: mbsaas

sections.description:
Browsers naturally start downloading tracking scripts, custom fonts, and video players the millisecond a page loads—long before any cookie banner can stop them.

The SaaSAudit plugin helps block supported trackers, fonts and embeds until a visitor consents, by intercepting and rewriting those elements on their way out of WordPress, without breaking your layout. How the plugin is configured, and what the privacy laws that apply to your site require, remain your responsibility: the plugin is a technical tool, not legal advice, and it does not guarantee compliance with any law.

Key Features:

  • True Pre-Consent Blocking: Holds back heavy or tracking elements (like YouTube, Vimeo, Google Maps, and Google Fonts) until the visitor clicks “Agree”.
  • Instant Script Injection: Places your official SaaSAudit script at the absolute top of your website’s <head> tag.
  • Full Caching Support: Compatible with page-caching plugins. It rewrites page data before the cache captures it, keeping cached content private.
  • Universal Compatibility: Plugs directly into the WP Consent API to broadcast visitor choices (functional, preferences, statistics, marketing) to your other installed plugins.
  • Respects Privacy Signals: Automatically honours global browser settings like Global Privacy Control (GPC).

External services

This integration relies explicitly on the SaaSAudit Consent Management cloud infrastructure to display banners and log user records securely. It requires an active account to function. The plugin communicates with the following external endpoints:

1. SaaSAudit API (https://consent.saasaudit.ai)

  • What it is: the SaaSAudit Consent Management service your account lives on. The plugin needs it to confirm your site is connected and to read the banner you designed.
  • When (from your site’s server, in PHP): when you connect the site, change a setting in the console, open the plugin’s settings page or press the check button; once a day while the site is connected (a safety net, so blocking rules found by a scan reach your site); and when SaaSAudit signals that a setting changed. Also when a page is built: the plugin asks for your banner settings (which consent model applies in which region) — your published banner settings — keeps the answer for five minutes (one minute if the request fails), so it is at most one small request per five minutes, never one per visitor.
  • Data sent: your site’s address, the Tenant ID and Site ID you entered when connecting, a one-time value used to confirm that you control the site’s address, and your site’s script token. No visitor data.
  • When (from the visitor’s browser): the consent script calls the same API to read the banner, to record a visitor’s choice and to count visits. Each request is listed under “Data transmitted by the client-side banner script” below.
  • Provider and legal terms: SaaSAudit.
    • Terms of Service: https://www.saasaudit.ai/legal/terms-of-service-policy
    • Privacy Policy: https://www.saasaudit.ai/legal/privacy-policy

2. SaaSAudit content delivery network (https://cdn.saasaudit.ai)

  • What it is: serves data only, never code: the descriptions of embedded services (small JSON files) that the consent dialogs show. All executable JavaScript, the consent script (cmp.js) and its c/ chunks, is bundled in this plugin and served from your own site; the plugin never loads or downloads JavaScript from the SaaSAudit CDN or any other remote server, and the script changes only when you update the plugin.
  • When: in the visitor’s browser, only when a visitor asks for more information about a service in the consent dialog.
  • Data sent: the request for one description file. Like any request, it exposes the visitor’s IP address to the server; nothing else is sent.
  • Provider and legal terms: SaaSAudit.
    • Terms of Service: https://www.saasaudit.ai/legal/terms-of-service-policy
    • Privacy Policy: https://www.saasaudit.ai/legal/privacy-policy

3. Hosted cookie declaration table (https://consent.saasaudit.ai/api/v1/cookie-policy/<your site's script token>, optionally followed by ?theme=light, dark or transparent)

  • What it is: your published cookie list, shown on a page of your site. Used only if you add the optional [saasaudit_cookie_policy] shortcode.
  • When: the shortcode prints an <iframe> pointing at that address, and the visitor’s browser requests it directly when the page is viewed. The plugin itself, in PHP, makes no request for it.
  • Data sent: the request exposes the visitor’s IP address to the API server, like any request. The page it returns loads nothing else and sets no cookie; it contains one small inline script that only tells your page how tall the table is, so the frame can fit it.
  • Provider and legal terms: SaaSAudit.
    • Terms of Service: https://www.saasaudit.ai/legal/terms-of-service-policy
    • Privacy Policy: https://www.saasaudit.ai/legal/privacy-policy

Other host names in the plugin’s code. The consent script reads Google Tag Manager script tags that are already on your page: when a visitor withdraws consent, it takes the Google Analytics measurement ID from such a tag (a googletagmanager.com address) to set the ga-disable-<ID> switch. This reads the page only and makes no request. The preference dialog also contains ordinary links to Google’s privacy pages (policies.google.com and business.safety.google, the latter for Google Business Data Responsibility) for sites that use Google services. The address www.w3.org/2000/svg is the standard name of the SVG format, used when the script draws its icons; it is a label, not a request. All other host names, in cmp.js, c/ and rules.php, are listed in the FAQ entry “Which host names does the plugin recognise?”.

Data Collection & Transparency

Data sent by this PHP plugin to the API:

  • The base site URL string (e.g., https://example.com).
  • The Tenant ID and Site ID you entered when connecting, so SaaSAudit can confirm they belong to this site.
  • A secure, temporary authorization value used exclusively to confirm domain ownership.
  • Your site’s script token, with the request for your banner settings.

Data returned from the API:

  • Active registration status, unique script installation tokens, your account’s name and plan (shown on the settings page after you connect), and your console’s Google Consent Mode preferences. No visitor metrics or personal information are sent or stored in this exchange.

Data transmitted by the client-side banner script (inside the browser):

  • The banner script runs in the visitor’s browser and calls the SaaSAudit API (https://consent.saasaudit.ai) in these cases. Like any request, each call exposes the visitor’s IP address to the API server; the sections below say what the service stores.
    • Reading your banner settings (GET /api/v1/domains/banner-config): when a page loads. Sends your site’s script token. Needed to show the banner you designed.
    • Finding the visitor’s country (GET /api/v1/domains/visitor-region): requested on every page load, at the same time as the banner settings, because the answer is needed before the page can be shown the right banner. It sends nothing but the request itself; the answer, the visitor’s country and state as told by SaaSAudit’s network provider, is returned to the browser. The browser uses it only when your banner’s rules depend on the region (a region-based or opt-out consent model, or the teen protections) and ignores it otherwise.
    • Install check (POST /api/v1/domains/beacon): at most once every 30 minutes per browser session. Sends your script token, whether the script loaded asynchronously, whether automatic blocking is on, and how many scripts ran before it. Needed to show in your console that the script is installed and to explain trackers that load early.
    • Session count (POST /api/v1/domains/session-beacon): when a new visit starts, at most once every 30 minutes per browser. Sends your script token and a random session ID, whatever the visitor’s consent. Needed to count sessions for your analytics and plan. Kept for 12 months.
    • Consent decision (POST /api/v1/domains/consent-decision): each time the visitor makes or changes a choice. Sends your script token, the choices, a random consent ID and whether a Global Privacy Control signal was detected; a choice made with the “Do Not Sell or Share” link, or applied automatically from a Global Privacy Control signal, is marked as such in the request address. The service adds an anonymous record containing the visitor’s country, a truncated IP address (the last part is removed, never the full address), and a browser/device classification. The full IP address is never logged or stored. Kept for the period in your subscription configuration (12 months by default). Needed as your record of consent.
    • Per-service decision (POST /api/v1/domains/service-consent): when the visitor allows or withdraws one embedded service, such as a video player. Sends your script token, the service’s name and whether it was allowed.
  • The newest build of the consent script is named in the banner settings; when it differs from the copy bundled in the plugin, the plugin’s settings page shows a notice asking you to update the plugin. Nothing is downloaded. The preference and information dialogs and the revisit icon are part of the plugin; only the service description files (data) are read from the SaaSAudit CDN when a visitor asks for them.
  • The plugin itself, in PHP, sends none of the visitor data above.
  • The plugin makes no request to any other third party. Embeds and scripts that are already on your pages (a video player, an analytics tag) are held back until the visitor allows them, and are then loaded by the visitor’s browser from their own provider as your page already asked; the links to those providers’ privacy policies shown in the preference dialog are ordinary links, not requests.

Lists of service names: rules.php, cmp.js and its c/ chunks contain lists of host names of well-known embeds and trackers (for example video players, maps, analytics and advertising tags). They are only compared with the scripts and embeds that your own pages already load, to hold those back until the visitor allows them. The plugin and the script make no request to those hosts and load nothing from them; they are not external services of this plugin.

Credit link: the plugin never shows a “Powered by SaaSAudit” credit or link on your site, and has no setting to turn one on. It injects no hidden tracking URLs or advertising tags into your content.

For more information, please review our terms:

  • SaaSAudit Consent Console
  • Official Terms of Service
  • Official Privacy Policy

By installing and configuring this plugin, you authorize these secure network requests to be processed. If you do not consent to these validation lookups, please remove the plugin files from your environment.

Public REST endpoints

The plugin adds two public REST routes under /wp-json/saasaudit/v1/, because SaaSAudit’s servers call them from outside your site:

  • GET /proof: returns a one-time value that SaaSAudit issued itself, only for the two minutes after a domain check starts; otherwise it answers 404 (and asks caches not to store the answer). It exposes nothing about your site or visitors.
  • POST /refresh: SaaSAudit’s signal that a setting changed in your console. It takes no input and carries no visitor data; it carries only the time, a one-time value and a signature made with a key SaaSAudit gave this site once the site proved it controls its address, and a request without a valid, recent, unused signature is refused. A valid one only makes the plugin run its normal connection check, which still has to prove that the site controls its address. It runs at most one check every two minutes (a signal that arrives sooner queues a single later check), so repeated calls cannot cause extra work.

Source Code

The plugin’s own code is plain, human-readable PHP and one small readable script, js/cookie-policy-resizer.js. The one generated PHP file, rules.php (the list of known embeds and trackers), is built from the same service catalog that SaaSAudit’s consent script uses; it is readable and shipped as is.

The plugin also includes a built copy of SaaSAudit’s consent script: cmp.js, with its c/ and assets/ folders. These files are minified JavaScript built from TypeScript. The complete unminified source is included in this plugin, in the source/ folder. The source repository is private, so the source and its build setup ship inside the plugin instead of a link:

  • cmp.js: built from source/cmp-loader/src/loader.ts.
  • c/prefs.*.js (the preference dialog): built from source/cmp-loader/src/chunks/prefs.ts.
  • c/info.*.js (the “More information” dialog): built from source/cmp-loader/src/chunks/info.ts.
  • source/cmp-loader/: the script’s TypeScript (src/), its service descriptions (services/), build scripts, rollup configs, package.json and package-lock.json.
  • source/shared/src/consent-catalog/: the catalogs of known services and trackers the script imports (tracker-rules.ts, embed-widgets.ts, tracker-catalog.ts and others).
  • source/cmp-loader/src/cdn-code.ts: a stub with nothing in it. The script SaaSAudit offers to sites that are not on WordPress can take its own files from a CDN; this plugin’s script is built without that code, so neither it nor its source loads any script from a remote server.
  • source/BUILD.txt: the same build instructions as below.

To rebuild cmp.js and c/*.js you need Node.js 22 (LTS) and npm:

cd source/cmp-loader && npm ci && GITHUB_SHA=<build id> CMP_API_BASE_URL=https://consent.saasaudit.ai npm run build

npm run build runs four steps in order: it builds the chunks (`rollup.chunks.config.mjs`), names each chunk by a hash of its contents (`scripts/hash-chunks.mjs`), builds the main script that lists those chunks (`rollup.config.mjs`), then writes a manifest (`scripts/generate-manifest.js`). That is why `c/prefs.*.js` is not a single separate compile; `source/BUILD.txt` lists the steps.

The result is in source/cmp-loader/dist/: cmp.js and c/*.js are the files shipped in the plugin, byte for byte, when built with the build id of this release. The build id is the commit recorded in the SAASAUDIT_BUNDLED_LOADER constant in rules.php (the script contains its first seven characters; any 40-character hexadecimal value that starts with them gives the same files). Each release of the plugin ships the source of the script it contains.
sections.installation:
You will need a SaaSAudit account to use this plugin (a free tier is available). Sign up at saasaudit.ai and add your website domain under Administration > Domains inside your console dashboard.

Install directly from WordPress:

  1. Navigate to Plugins > Add New in your dashboard and search for SaaSAudit.
  2. Find SaaSAudit, click Install Now, and then click Activate.
  3. After activating, the plugin takes you to Settings > SaaSAudit and does nothing on your site until you connect it. In your SaaSAudit console, open Administration > Domains: the Tenant ID and the Site ID are shown under your domain, each with a Copy button (they are also in Install code > WordPress). Copy both, paste them on the settings page and click Connect. SaaSAudit checks that they belong to this site, and the page then shows which account it is connected to. If you do not have an account yet, the settings page has a “Sign up and choose a plan” link to our pricing page.
  4. Note: If you previously pasted a SaaSAudit script tag manually into your theme files, please delete it now to avoid duplicates.

Manual upload:

  1. Download the plugin .zip package from the official WordPress.org Directory.
  2. Go to Plugins > Add New > Upload Plugin in your dashboard.
  3. Select the file, click Install Now, and activate it.

Troubleshooting Connections & Staging Sites:

If connecting fails, check that you copied both IDs from the domain that matches this site’s exact address under Administration > Domains in the SaaSAudit console. A message such as “These IDs are not the ones of this site” means one of the IDs belongs to a different domain or account. Once connected, Check connection asks SaaSAudit again.

For advanced developers configuring sandboxes, you can manually override the API and CDN endpoints (the CDN serves data only, never the script), and the sign-up and sign-in links shown on the settings page, using these wp-config.php constants: SAASAUDIT_CDN_BASE_URL, SAASAUDIT_API_BASE_URL, SAASAUDIT_SIGNUP_URL and SAASAUDIT_SIGNIN_URL (the last two must be https addresses).
sections.faq:
Do I need a SaaSAudit account to use this?

Yes. The plugin acts as a bridge to deploy and manage the custom consent banner designed inside your SaaSAudit account dashboard. It does nothing until you connect it with your Tenant ID and Site ID, and it will not execute anything without an active domain subscription (Free or Paid).

How do I show my cookie list on a page?

Add the shortcode [saasaudit_cookie_policy] to the page. It shows the cookie table from your published banner, sized to fit. Use [saasaudit_cookie_policy theme="dark"] (or light, or transparent) to match your page. The cookie table is part of the Plus plan.

Why isn’t my consent banner showing after I installed the plugin or added the script?

Work through these in order:

  1. Click “Check installation” in your SaaSAudit dashboard. If it says the script is not in the page, the cause is a cache or a missing install. A dashboard that says “Banner not showing” means the same.
  2. Clear every cache, in all three places: your caching or performance plugin (WP Rocket, LiteSpeed, W3 Total Cache and similar), your host’s cache (Pantheon, WP Engine, Kinsta, SiteGround and similar) and your CDN (for example Cloudflare’s page cache). Pages cached before you connected the plugin keep serving the old HTML until they are cleared. The plugin clears the common caches itself whenever your banner’s install code changes, so purge by hand only if your host has a cache the plugin does not know about. Some caches keep a separate copy of each page per compression type, so the page can look right in your browser while other visitors still get the old one.
  3. Test in a fresh Incognito or Private window. After you click Accept or Reject, your browser remembers the choice and does not show the banner again until that cookie is cleared or expires.
  4. Check the domain. The address of your live site must match the one under Administration > Domains exactly, including www against non-www and staging subdomains. A paused domain serves no banner.
  5. Check publishing. If you have never published, visitors see the standard default banner. If you saved changes, visitors still see the last published version until you click Publish. The dashboard shows “Banner changes not published” while changes are waiting.
  6. Check your region settings. The banner can behave differently by visitor country, so test from a country your settings target.

Performance plugins can interfere too. Exclude the SaaSAudit script from anything that defers, delays, combines or self-hosts JavaScript (for example WP Rocket’s “Delay JavaScript”, Autoptimize and Cloudflare Rocket Loader).

If it still does not show, send support your domain, the page URL and what “Check installation” says.

Does the banner show on every visit?

No. After a visitor chooses, it stays hidden until they clear their cookies or their choice expires. Use a private window to see it again.

Why does my banner look different from the preview in my dashboard?

Make sure the SaaSAudit script is the first script in the head of your page. This plugin does that itself once it is connected. Exclude it from any feature that defers, minifies or delays JavaScript. The banner protects its buttons from common theme button styles, but a broad rule in your theme (global button, input or typography styles, especially with !important) can still win. Inspect the element in your browser’s developer tools to find the rule, or send support the page URL.

Why is my cookie list empty or short?

A scan runs when you add a domain. It visits your pages twice: once as a new visitor with no consent, and once as a visitor who accepted everything, so tags that wait for consent are found too. Visitors’ own choices never change the list. If the list looks wrong, click “Re-scan”. On a site with another cookie banner, tags that only load after that banner’s Accept may not be found; tell support and we will look.

What happens when a new cookie is found?

A cookie with a category and a description is added to your banner automatically, with no need to publish, and reaches visitors within a few minutes. A cookie with no category or no description waits for your review on the Cookies page. The dashboard and the Cookies page show how many new cookies and services the latest scan found.

When is a newly found tracker blocked on my site?

When a scan finds a tracker that SaaSAudit can identify from a trusted source, it is held back until visitors agree. The consent banner on your pages starts holding it within a few minutes. The plugin also holds it back before the page reaches the browser once the plugin has refreshed its blocking rules: SaaSAudit asks it to refresh after each scan, and it asks again once a day on its own. After a refresh that changed the rules, the plugin empties the page caches it knows about. A refresh can be delayed (a firewall, a busy site), and a page that a cache or CDN already holds is served as it was until that cache is emptied or expires. So protection for a tracker that was only just found is not guaranteed at the moment of the scan.

Can I re-scan whenever I like?

Paid plans can re-scan on demand. The Free plan scans when you add the domain and does not offer on-demand re-scans. After a scan the button shows “Re-scan in” and a countdown for a few minutes, then becomes available again.

Do I have to reinstall the plugin, or clear caches, to get updates?

No. What visitors see (the banner’s look and texts, and its cookie list) comes from your SaaSAudit account and reaches your site by itself. You do nothing in WordPress.

Updates to the plugin itself arrive as WordPress’s normal “Update available” on the Plugins page. If you downloaded the plugin from your SaaSAudit dashboard, automatic updates are switched on for it when you activate it (you can switch them off on the Plugins page, and that choice is kept). If you installed it from the WordPress.org directory, turn on “Enable auto-updates” for it on the Plugins page.

I pasted the SaaSAudit script by hand instead of using the plugin. Do I need to do anything?

No. The script is served from SaaSAudit, so improvements reach your site by themselves. The only exception is a caching or performance plugin that combines, minifies or self-hosts third-party scripts: it can keep serving an old copy until you purge its cache.

Does it conflict with my caching plugins?

No. The plugin rewrites the page’s HTML before your page-caching plugin captures it, so cached pages carry the same changes. A page cached before the plugin was connected, or before a setting changed, keeps its old HTML until the cache is purged.

Can I tell the plugin a visitor’s age?

Yes, if your site knows it (for example from a member’s profile). Return “under13”, “under16” or “adult” from the saasaudit_consent_age_band filter and the consent script treats that visitor accordingly from the first paint: for example add_filter( 'saasaudit_consent_age_band', fn() => is_user_logged_in() && my_user_is_teen() ? 'under16' : '' );. Pages that differ per visitor must not be served to other visitors from a page cache. This only applies when the banner’s Teen privacy setting is “Ages from my site”.

What should I do if the settings page says “Not connected”?

Enter your Tenant ID and Site ID and click Connect. Make sure your website’s exact live URL is added under Administration > Domains in your SaaSAudit dashboard (note that staging domains must be added individually). If it still fails, check whether your site uses a hard login wall, tight firewall rules, or has disabled the default WordPress REST API.

I am running an older pre-release version of “SaaSAudit Consent”.

Please completely deactivate and delete the legacy test package before installing this official release. If both versions run concurrently, this plugin will display an admin warning and safely disable its features to prevent site loops.

Should I still paste the original integration script into my theme editor?

No. This plugin handles the asset loading process for you dynamically. Pasting code into your theme will create a redundant second copy on your live pages.

Where is the unminified source code and build setup for the JavaScript files?

All distributed JavaScript files (cmp.js, c/prefs.*.js and c/info.*.js) are built from unminified TypeScript that is included in this plugin, under source/cmp-loader/ and source/shared/. Step-by-step build instructions (Node.js 22, npm ci, then the build script) are in source/BUILD.txt and in the “Source Code” section below. The source repository is private, so the source ships inside the plugin.

Does this plugin load scripts, fonts or embeds from Google, YouTube, Vimeo or Tag Manager?

The plugin itself loads nothing from them. Those host names are in the catalog the plugin uses to recognise, and hold back until the visitor consents, scripts and embeds that your site already has on its pages. After a visitor consents, their browser loads an embed or script from its own provider, exactly as your page already asked it to. The catalog is in source/shared/src/consent-catalog/ (tracker-rules.ts, embed-widgets.ts, tracker-catalog.ts).

Which host names does the plugin recognise?

The plugin and its consent script compare these host names with the scripts and embeds that a page already loads, to hold them back until the visitor allows them. They are names to match, not addresses the plugin fetches from. The list is generated from the same catalog as the plugin’s code.

short_description: Automatically blocks tracking cookies, scripts, embedded videos, and maps on your site until visitors explicitly give their consent.
description:
Browsers naturally start downloading tracking scripts, custom fonts, and video players the millisecond a page loads—long before any cookie banner can stop them.

The SaaSAudit plugin helps block supported trackers, fonts and embeds until a visitor consents, by intercepting and rewriting those elements on their way out of WordPress, without breaking your layout. How the plugin is configured, and what the privacy laws that apply to your site require, remain your responsibility: the plugin is a technical tool, not legal advice, and it does not guarantee compliance with any law.

Key Features:

  • True Pre-Consent Blocking: Holds back heavy or tracking elements (like YouTube, Vimeo, Google Maps, and Google Fonts) until the visitor clicks “Agree”.
  • Instant Script Injection: Places your official SaaSAudit script at the absolute top of your website’s <head> tag.
  • Full Caching Support: Compatible with page-caching plugins. It rewrites page data before the cache captures it, keeping cached content private.
  • Universal Compatibility: Plugs directly into the WP Consent API to broadcast visitor choices (functional, preferences, statistics, marketing) to your other installed plugins.
  • Respects Privacy Signals: Automatically honours global browser settings like Global Privacy Control (GPC).

External services

This integration relies explicitly on the SaaSAudit Consent Management cloud infrastructure to display banners and log user records securely. It requires an active account to function. The plugin communicates with the following external endpoints:

1. SaaSAudit API (https://consent.saasaudit.ai)

  • What it is: the SaaSAudit Consent Management service your account lives on. The plugin needs it to confirm your site is connected and to read the banner you designed.
  • When (from your site’s server, in PHP): when you connect the site, change a setting in the console, open the plugin’s settings page or press the check button; once a day while the site is connected (a safety net, so blocking rules found by a scan reach your site); and when SaaSAudit signals that a setting changed. Also when a page is built: the plugin asks for your banner settings (which consent model applies in which region) — your published banner settings — keeps the answer for five minutes (one minute if the request fails), so it is at most one small request per five minutes, never one per visitor.
  • Data sent: your site’s address, the Tenant ID and Site ID you entered when connecting, a one-time value used to confirm that you control the site’s address, and your site’s script token. No visitor data.
  • When (from the visitor’s browser): the consent script calls the same API to read the banner, to record a visitor’s choice and to count visits. Each request is listed under “Data transmitted by the client-side banner script” below.
  • Provider and legal terms: SaaSAudit.
    • Terms of Service: https://www.saasaudit.ai/legal/terms-of-service-policy
    • Privacy Policy: https://www.saasaudit.ai/legal/privacy-policy

2. SaaSAudit content delivery network (https://cdn.saasaudit.ai)

  • What it is: serves data only, never code: the descriptions of embedded services (small JSON files) that the consent dialogs show. All executable JavaScript, the consent script (cmp.js) and its c/ chunks, is bundled in this plugin and served from your own site; the plugin never loads or downloads JavaScript from the SaaSAudit CDN or any other remote server, and the script changes only when you update the plugin.
  • When: in the visitor’s browser, only when a visitor asks for more information about a service in the consent dialog.
  • Data sent: the request for one description file. Like any request, it exposes the visitor’s IP address to the server; nothing else is sent.
  • Provider and legal terms: SaaSAudit.
    • Terms of Service: https://www.saasaudit.ai/legal/terms-of-service-policy
    • Privacy Policy: https://www.saasaudit.ai/legal/privacy-policy

3. Hosted cookie declaration table (https://consent.saasaudit.ai/api/v1/cookie-policy/<your site's script token>, optionally followed by ?theme=light, dark or transparent)

  • What it is: your published cookie list, shown on a page of your site. Used only if you add the optional [saasaudit_cookie_policy] shortcode.
  • When: the shortcode prints an <iframe> pointing at that address, and the visitor’s browser requests it directly when the page is viewed. The plugin itself, in PHP, makes no request for it.
  • Data sent: the request exposes the visitor’s IP address to the API server, like any request. The page it returns loads nothing else and sets no cookie; it contains one small inline script that only tells your page how tall the table is, so the frame can fit it.
  • Provider and legal terms: SaaSAudit.
    • Terms of Service: https://www.saasaudit.ai/legal/terms-of-service-policy
    • Privacy Policy: https://www.saasaudit.ai/legal/privacy-policy

Other host names in the plugin’s code. The consent script reads Google Tag Manager script tags that are already on your page: when a visitor withdraws consent, it takes the Google Analytics measurement ID from such a tag (a googletagmanager.com address) to set the ga-disable-<ID> switch. This reads the page only and makes no request. The preference dialog also contains ordinary links to Google’s privacy pages (policies.google.com and business.safety.google, the latter for Google Business Data Responsibility) for sites that use Google services. The address www.w3.org/2000/svg is the standard name of the SVG format, used when the script draws its icons; it is a label, not a request. All other host names, in cmp.js, c/ and rules.php, are listed in the FAQ entry “Which host names does the plugin recognise?”.

Data Collection & Transparency

Data sent by this PHP plugin to the API:

  • The base site URL string (e.g., https://example.com).
  • The Tenant ID and Site ID you entered when connecting, so SaaSAudit can confirm they belong to this site.
  • A secure, temporary authorization value used exclusively to confirm domain ownership.
  • Your site’s script token, with the request for your banner settings.

Data returned from the API:

  • Active registration status, unique script installation tokens, your account’s name and plan (shown on the settings page after you connect), and your console’s Google Consent Mode preferences. No visitor metrics or personal information are sent or stored in this exchange.

Data transmitted by the client-side banner script (inside the browser):

  • The banner script runs in the visitor’s browser and calls the SaaSAudit API (https://consent.saasaudit.ai) in these cases. Like any request, each call exposes the visitor’s IP address to the API server; the sections below say what the service stores.
    • Reading your banner settings (GET /api/v1/domains/banner-config): when a page loads. Sends your site’s script token. Needed to show the banner you designed.
    • Finding the visitor’s country (GET /api/v1/domains/visitor-region): requested on every page load, at the same time as the banner settings, because the answer is needed before the page can be shown the right banner. It sends nothing but the request itself; the answer, the visitor’s country and state as told by SaaSAudit’s network provider, is returned to the browser. The browser uses it only when your banner’s rules depend on the region (a region-based or opt-out consent model, or the teen protections) and ignores it otherwise.
    • Install check (POST /api/v1/domains/beacon): at most once every 30 minutes per browser session. Sends your script token, whether the script loaded asynchronously, whether automatic blocking is on, and how many scripts ran before it. Needed to show in your console that the script is installed and to explain trackers that load early.
    • Session count (POST /api/v1/domains/session-beacon): when a new visit starts, at most once every 30 minutes per browser. Sends your script token and a random session ID, whatever the visitor’s consent. Needed to count sessions for your analytics and plan. Kept for 12 months.
    • Consent decision (POST /api/v1/domains/consent-decision): each time the visitor makes or changes a choice. Sends your script token, the choices, a random consent ID and whether a Global Privacy Control signal was detected; a choice made with the “Do Not Sell or Share” link, or applied automatically from a Global Privacy Control signal, is marked as such in the request address. The service adds an anonymous record containing the visitor’s country, a truncated IP address (the last part is removed, never the full address), and a browser/device classification. The full IP address is never logged or stored. Kept for the period in your subscription configuration (12 months by default). Needed as your record of consent.
    • Per-service decision (POST /api/v1/domains/service-consent): when the visitor allows or withdraws one embedded service, such as a video player. Sends your script token, the service’s name and whether it was allowed.
  • The newest build of the consent script is named in the banner settings; when it differs from the copy bundled in the plugin, the plugin’s settings page shows a notice asking you to update the plugin. Nothing is downloaded. The preference and information dialogs and the revisit icon are part of the plugin; only the service description files (data) are read from the SaaSAudit CDN when a visitor asks for them.
  • The plugin itself, in PHP, sends none of the visitor data above.
  • The plugin makes no request to any other third party. Embeds and scripts that are already on your pages (a video player, an analytics tag) are held back until the visitor allows them, and are then loaded by the visitor’s browser from their own provider as your page already asked; the links to those providers’ privacy policies shown in the preference dialog are ordinary links, not requests.

Lists of service names: rules.php, cmp.js and its c/ chunks contain lists of host names of well-known embeds and trackers (for example video players, maps, analytics and advertising tags). They are only compared with the scripts and embeds that your own pages already load, to hold those back until the visitor allows them. The plugin and the script make no request to those hosts and load nothing from them; they are not external services of this plugin.

Credit link: the plugin never shows a “Powered by SaaSAudit” credit or link on your site, and has no setting to turn one on. It injects no hidden tracking URLs or advertising tags into your content.

For more information, please review our terms:

  • SaaSAudit Consent Console
  • Official Terms of Service
  • Official Privacy Policy

By installing and configuring this plugin, you authorize these secure network requests to be processed. If you do not consent to these validation lookups, please remove the plugin files from your environment.

Public REST endpoints

The plugin adds two public REST routes under /wp-json/saasaudit/v1/, because SaaSAudit’s servers call them from outside your site:

  • GET /proof: returns a one-time value that SaaSAudit issued itself, only for the two minutes after a domain check starts; otherwise it answers 404 (and asks caches not to store the answer). It exposes nothing about your site or visitors.
  • POST /refresh: SaaSAudit’s signal that a setting changed in your console. It takes no input and carries no visitor data; it carries only the time, a one-time value and a signature made with a key SaaSAudit gave this site once the site proved it controls its address, and a request without a valid, recent, unused signature is refused. A valid one only makes the plugin run its normal connection check, which still has to prove that the site controls its address. It runs at most one check every two minutes (a signal that arrives sooner queues a single later check), so repeated calls cannot cause extra work.

Source Code

The plugin’s own code is plain, human-readable PHP and one small readable script, js/cookie-policy-resizer.js. The one generated PHP file, rules.php (the list of known embeds and trackers), is built from the same service catalog that SaaSAudit’s consent script uses; it is readable and shipped as is.

The plugin also includes a built copy of SaaSAudit’s consent script: cmp.js, with its c/ and assets/ folders. These files are minified JavaScript built from TypeScript. The complete unminified source is included in this plugin, in the source/ folder. The source repository is private, so the source and its build setup ship inside the plugin instead of a link:

  • cmp.js: built from source/cmp-loader/src/loader.ts.
  • c/prefs.*.js (the preference dialog): built from source/cmp-loader/src/chunks/prefs.ts.
  • c/info.*.js (the “More information” dialog): built from source/cmp-loader/src/chunks/info.ts.
  • source/cmp-loader/: the script’s TypeScript (src/), its service descriptions (services/), build scripts, rollup configs, package.json and package-lock.json.
  • source/shared/src/consent-catalog/: the catalogs of known services and trackers the script imports (tracker-rules.ts, embed-widgets.ts, tracker-catalog.ts and others).
  • source/cmp-loader/src/cdn-code.ts: a stub with nothing in it. The script SaaSAudit offers to sites that are not on WordPress can take its own files from a CDN; this plugin’s script is built without that code, so neither it nor its source loads any script from a remote server.
  • source/BUILD.txt: the same build instructions as below.

To rebuild cmp.js and c/*.js you need Node.js 22 (LTS) and npm:

cd source/cmp-loader && npm ci && GITHUB_SHA=<build id> CMP_API_BASE_URL=https://consent.saasaudit.ai npm run build

npm run build runs four steps in order: it builds the chunks (`rollup.chunks.config.mjs`), names each chunk by a hash of its contents (`scripts/hash-chunks.mjs`), builds the main script that lists those chunks (`rollup.config.mjs`), then writes a manifest (`scripts/generate-manifest.js`). That is why `c/prefs.*.js` is not a single separate compile; `source/BUILD.txt` lists the steps.

The result is in source/cmp-loader/dist/: cmp.js and c/*.js are the files shipped in the plugin, byte for byte, when built with the build id of this release. The build id is the commit recorded in the SAASAUDIT_BUNDLED_LOADER constant in rules.php (the script contains its first seven characters; any 40-character hexadecimal value that starts with them gives the same files). Each release of the plugin ships the source of the script it contains.
